title: Circuit Tracers and Breaker Finders

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Office with a hardwired fixture, ceiling tile lifted; lighting panel with an outdated directory taped inside the door. Medium shot.
scenes.on_screen: Job Mindset: hazards = wrong breaker, second sources, energized connections | trace, lock out, verify every conductor
scenes.says: Before you can lock out a fixture, you have to know which breaker feeds it, and panel directories are often wrong. The hazards: the wrong breaker, a second source, and energized connections while tracing. So plan it: check the schedule and lighting plan, check your tracer's voltage rating, bring your lockout kit and meter. And remember, a tracer never replaces verification.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.on_screen: Don't flip breakers to see what goes out
scenes.says: Turning breakers off one by one to see what goes out can shut down critical equipment, computer rooms or emergency lighting, and it annoys customers. A tracer finds the breaker quickly with less disruption. For receptacle circuits, a plug-in breaker finder plugs in and injects a signal, and you sweep the receiver over the breakers. It's usually 120 volts only.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Tech plugs a breaker finder into a receptacle, sweeps the receiver over breaker handles; one lights up.
scenes.on_screen: Plug-in breaker finder: 120 V receptacle circuits
scenes.says: Here's the plug-in finder on a receptacle. Sweep the receiver along the breaker handles, and you get one strong signal. For a hardwired fixture, you need an energized circuit tracer. Read the transmitter's ratings first. Many are 120 volts only. Connecting a 120 volt transmitter to a 277 volt circuit can destroy it and create a hazard.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Tech in PPE at the fixture junction box clips the transmitter to hot and neutral; transmitter indicator shows it's transmitting.
scenes.on_screen: 1 Prepare | 2 Access safely (energized work: PPE, supervisor direction) | 3 Connect transmitter hot to neutral
scenes.says: Prepare: check the schedule and plan, note the panel and its voltage. Connecting to energized conductors is energized work, so PPE per our program and supervisor direction. Where you can, use a method that avoids opening splices. Connect the transmitter per its instructions, commonly hot to neutral, and confirm it shows it's connected and transmitting.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: At the panel, tech sweeps the receiver, lowering sensitivity until one breaker gives a strong signal; checks adjacent breakers.
scenes.on_screen: 4 Sweep, lower sensitivity | 5 Confirm on adjacent breakers | 6 Remove the transmitter
scenes.says: At the panel, calibrate the receiver and sweep the breaker handles. Lower the sensitivity as you narrow down, until only one breaker gives a strong signal. Check adjacent breakers. A strong signal on two can mean coupling, a multiwire circuit or a tandem breaker. Then remove the transmitter before de-energizing, or follow the tool's instructions.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Above the ceiling: tech sweeps the receiver slowly along the wiring path; signal peaks over the conductor, fades at EMT, returns at a box.
scenes.on_screen: Tracing: sweep slowly | signal peaks over the conductor | metal raceway weakens it
scenes.says: The receiver can also follow the wiring above a ceiling. Hold it close and sweep slowly. The signal peaks right over the conductor and drops off to the sides. Metal raceway shields it, so you may lose it through EMT or MC, then pick it up again at boxes. Use this to find hidden junction boxes, or which fixtures share a circuit.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Tech applies lock and tag to the identified breaker, then verifies live-dead-live at the fixture on all conductors.
scenes.on_screen: 7 Lock out | 8 Verify all conductors, live-dead-live | still live? Stop. Re-trace. | 9 Update the directory
scenes.says: Lock out the identified breaker per our LOTO procedure. Then verify absence of voltage at the fixture on all conductors with a tested meter, live-dead-live. The tracer tells you which breaker probably feeds it. Only the meter after lockout tells you it's dead. Fixtures can have a second source, like an unswitched emergency feed. Still live? Stop and re-trace. Then update the directory.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Matthew beside the panel, medium shot.
scenes.on_screen: Continuity method: remove the jumper before re-energizing
scenes.says: No tracer? On a de-energized circuit, you can match conductors with a jumper to a known reference at one end and continuity at the other. Just remove the jumper before re-energizing. A forgotten jumper is a dead short. Now read the lesson and take the quiz.

production_notes: Per the lesson's video suggestion: plug-in breaker finder on a receptacle, energized circuit tracer at a fixture junction box (tech in PPE, transmitter rated for the circuit voltage), receiver tracing above a ceiling, then lockout and live-dead-live verification. Use a mock panel directory with no customer names.
